title: Body and health
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: yuʾlimunī is M6's backwards verb doing the job it does best: yuʾlimunī raʾsī is "my head pains me". The body part is the SUBJECT and it already carries the possessive -ī, so the sentence says whose head it is exactly once. Feminine parts take tuʾlimunī — tuʾlimunī rijlī — for the same reason tuʿjibunī followed al-mūsīqā.

qad + a past verb is what has happened and still matters: qad akhadhtu ad-dawāʾ, "I have taken the medicine". It is a PARTICLE, not a tense — nothing about the verb changes and the particle does all the work. Health is where you meet it first, because a symptom is by definition still true.

mundhu is "for" or "since", and the trap is the TENSE beside it: yuʾlimunī raʾsī mundhu yawmayn — a PRESENT verb where English needs a perfect, "my head HAS hurt for two days". Arabic reasons that it still hurts, so it is still present. This is the mirror of the qad rule, and the two do not conflict.
A symptom is a thing you have, exactly as a feeling was in M6: ʿindī ḥumma, ʿindī suʿāl, ʿindī zukām. No verb, no adjective, just L1-M7's ʿindī and the noun.

The two sentences a pharmacy needs are built from frames you already own: hal ʿindaka dawāʾ li-aṣ-ṣudāʿ? and kam marra fī al-yawm? The li- is L1-M9's, hal is L1-M2's, kam is L1-M8's. Nothing here is a new question shape.

words.note: Pains me. Same machine as M6's yuʿjibunī: the body part is the subject, you are the -nī. tuʾlimunī for a feminine part.
Head, the bare noun. r is a sun letter, so the article assimilates: ar-raʾs.
My head — raʾs plus the -ī you have carried since ismī. In this frame the -ī is the only owner marker the sentence gets.

sentences.trap: Two words in Arabic, three in English. Do not add a second owner: raʾsī already says "my", so anā yuʾlimunī raʾsī is one "my" too many.
sentences.sound: yuʾ-li-MU-nee RAʾ-see — the ʾ is a stop in the throat, so raʾsī is two beats, not "rah-see".

variations.cue: My head hurts a lot
variations.changed: how much: jiddan added

variations.cue: My leg hurts
variations.changed: which part — and rijl is feminine, so the verb turns to tuʾlimunī

mistake.why: The English subject smuggled in front. The -nī inside the verb is already "me" and the -ī on raʾsī is already "my": yuʾlimunī raʾsī.

sentences.usage: The first thing you say to a doctor, a pharmacist or a host who asks why you are quiet.
sentences.mnemonic: The head does the hurting. You only receive it.

sentences.cue: My back has hurt for two days

words.note: Back. ẓ is a sun letter: aẓ-ẓahr. Not the ẓuhr of L2-M6's clock, which is the same letters and a different word.
My back — ẓahr with the -ī of S01's raʾsī. Its own surface, because that is the form the frame actually shows.
For, since. The verb beside it stays PRESENT: yuʾlimunī … mundhu yawmayn is "has hurt for two days", because it still hurts.
Two days — yawm in the dual, one word for the pair. Take it as vocabulary here; the dual as a system belongs to L4.

sentences.trap: English says "has hurt" and reaches for a perfect. Arabic keeps the present because the pain has not stopped. Putting a past verb here says it hurt and then stopped, which is not what you want at a clinic.
sentences.sound: MUN-dhu yaw-MAYN — the dh is the soft one in "this", and yawmayn ends on a clean -ayn.

variations.cue: My head has hurt for two days
variations.changed: which part: ẓahrī → raʾsī

variations.cue: My stomach hurts today
variations.changed: duration → a plain today

mistake.why: A past verb after mundhu closes the pain off in the past. Keep the present: yuʾlimunī ẓahrī mundhu yawmayn.

sentences.usage: The sentence that gets a doctor's attention, because it carries how long as well as where.

words.note: A particle, not a tense. qad + past = it happened and it still counts. The verb does not change at all — qad does the whole job.
I took — the past of L1-M9's khudh. akhadha for he, akhadhat for she, same -tu ending you know from dhahabtu.
Medicine. d is a sun letter: ad-dawāʾ. The plural adwiya is what a pharmacy shelf is labelled.

sentences.trap: English builds the perfect out of two verbs, "have taken". Arabic keeps one verb and puts a small word in front of it. Nothing about akhadhtu is different from the plain past.
sentences.sound: QAD a-KHADH-tu — qad is short and unstressed, almost leaning on the verb.

variations.cue: He has taken the medicine
variations.changed: who: akhadhtu → akhadha

variations.cue: I have arrived at the hospital
variations.changed: which verb: L2-M10's waṣaltu takes qad the same way

mistake.why: qad wants the PAST beside it for this meaning. With a present verb it says something much weaker, closer to "I may take". qad akhadhtu ad-dawāʾ.

sentences.usage: What you tell a doctor before they prescribe anything, and what you tell a worried friend.
sentences.mnemonic: qad is one small word doing what English needs two for.

sentences.cue: I have a fever and a cough

words.note: Fever. ḥ is a moon letter, so the article stays al-: al-ḥumma. Held by ʿindī, exactly like M6's khawf.
Cough — a noun in Arabic, never a verb the way English uses it. s is a sun letter: as-suʿāl.

sentences.trap: English can say "I am coughing" with a verb. Arabic hands you a noun and lets ʿindī hold it, which is one less shape to learn, not one more.
sentences.sound: ʿIN-dee ḤUM-ma wa su-ʿAAL — the wa is glued to the next word and never stressed.

variations.cue: I have a fever today
variations.changed: one symptom instead of two

variations.cue: You have a cough
variations.changed: who has it: ʿindī → ʿindaka

mistake.why: "I am fever." A symptom is a thing you hold, not a thing you are: ʿindī ḥumma.

sentences.usage: The two-symptom sentence that gets you seen — at a clinic, a pharmacy or the front desk of a hotel.
sentences.mnemonic: Symptoms are luggage. ʿindī carries them.

sentences.cue: I have a cold and I am not well

words.note: A head cold. z is a sun letter: az-zukām. Nothing to do with bārid, which is a temperature and not an illness.

sentences.trap: bārid is cold weather or a cold drink. The illness is zukām, a different word entirely — the English pun does not exist in Arabic.
sentences.sound: zu-KAAM, the long ā held; wa-LAS-tu bi-KHAYR runs together as one phrase.

variations.cue: I have a cough and I am not well
variations.changed: which symptom: zukām → suʿāl

variations.cue: I have had a cold for two days
variations.changed: the second half → S02's duration frame

mistake.why: That is "I have a cold thing" — the English word borrowed straight across. The illness is zukām: ʿindī zukām.

sentences.usage: The full answer to kayfa ḥāluka when the honest answer is not bi-khayr — and it uses M6's lastu to say so.
sentences.mnemonic: bārid is the weather; zukām is what the weather did to you.

sentences.cue: Do you have medicine for a headache?

words.note: L1-M9's li- on L2-M8's ṣudāʿ, its first outing as one word. ṣ is a sun letter, so the article assimilates: li-aṣ-ṣudāʿ.

sentences.trap: Nothing here is new grammar — hal from L1-M2, ʿindaka from L1-M7, li- from L1-M9, ṣudāʿ from L2-M8. What is new is that a whole pharmacy request falls out of four things you already own.
sentences.sound: hal ʿIN-da-ka da-WAAʾ liṣ-ṣu-DAAʿ — the li- and the ṣ run together with no gap.

variations.cue: Do you have medicine for a headache?
variations.changed: who you are asking: ʿindaka → ʿindaki

variations.cue: Do you have medicine?
variations.changed: the li- phrase dropped, when you cannot name the problem

mistake.why: Two bare nouns touching is an iḍāfa (L3-M2) and reads as "headache medicine" in the sense of medicine belonging to a headache. For "for", you need the li-: li-aṣ-ṣudāʿ.

sentences.usage: Said at a pharmacy counter, exactly as written, and the ṣ can be swapped for any symptom you have a word for.
sentences.mnemonic: li- is what "for" is made of.

words.note: One occasion. After kam the noun stays SINGULAR — kam marra, never kam marrāt. marratayn is the dual, twice.

sentences.trap: English says "how many timeS". Arabic counts with kam and then leaves the noun singular, which feels wrong for exactly one sentence and then feels normal.
sentences.sound: kam MAR-ra fil-YAWM — the doubled r is held for a beat.

variations.cue: How many times before bed?
variations.changed: the window: fī al-yawm → qabla an-nawm

variations.cue: Twice a day
variations.changed: the question turned into its answer

mistake.why: kam takes the singular. The plural after it is the English habit showing: kam marra fī al-yawm.

sentences.usage: The second half of every pharmacy conversation, and the question the label answers.
sentences.mnemonic: kam counts; the noun stays one.

sentences.cue: I have to go to the doctor

words.note: Doctor. ṭ is a sun letter: aṭ-ṭabīb. ṭabība for a woman — an ordinary noun with an ordinary feminine.

sentences.trap: The frame is L3-M2's yajibu an, untouched. Only the destination is new, and aṭ-ṭabīb means the person, not the surgery.
sentences.sound: YAJ-i-bu an ADH-hab i-laṭ-ṭa-BEEB — the ilā swallows into the article.

variations.cue: I have to go to the hospital
variations.changed: where: the doctor → the hospital

variations.cue: I have to go to the pharmacy
variations.changed: where: the doctor → the pharmacy

mistake.why: yajibu needs its an before the verb — that is L3-M2's rule and health does not suspend it: yajibu an adhhab.

sentences.usage: The decision said out loud, to yourself or to whoever is asking why you cancelled.

sentences.cue: The pharmacy is near the hospital

words.note: Pharmacy. ṣ is a sun letter: aṣ-ṣaydaliyya. Feminine, so the adjective beside it takes -a: qarība.
Hospital. m is a moon letter: al-mustashfā. The final -ā never changes, whatever the sentence does around it.

sentences.trap: "Near" is an adjective here, not a preposition, so it agrees: aṣ-ṣaydaliyya qarība, al-mustashfā qarīb. What follows it is min, not ilā.

variations.cue: The pharmacy is near the house
variations.changed: near what: the hospital → the house

variations.cue: The hospital is near here
variations.changed: who is near what — and the adjective loses its -a

mistake.why: ṣaydaliyya is feminine, so the adjective must be qarība. The -a is not decoration; it is what tells you which noun the adjective belongs to.

sentences.usage: The answer you will be given when you ask where to fill a prescription.
sentences.mnemonic: qarīb min — near FROM, not near to.

sentences.cue: My stomach hurts, and my hand too

words.note: Stomach. b is a moon letter: al-baṭn. This is the belly you point at, not the digestive organ a doctor would name.
My stomach — baṭn with the -ī of S01's raʾsī. Its own surface, because that is the form the frame shows.
Hand. y is a moon letter: al-yad. Feminine, like most paired body parts, so it takes tuʾlimunī.
My hand — yad with the same -ī. Two letters in Arabic and a whole English phrase.
Leg or foot — Arabic does not split them. r is a sun letter: ar-rijl. Feminine, so tuʾlimunī rijlī.
My leg — rijl with the -ī, seen in S01's second variation. Feminine, so the verb beside it is tuʾlimunī.

sentences.trap: The second half needs no second verb: wa yadī ayḍan borrows the yuʾlimunī in front of it. Repeating the verb is not wrong, only heavy.
sentences.sound: yuʾ-li-MU-nee BAṬ-nee, wa ya-DEE AY-ḍan — a real pause at the comma.

variations.cue: My back hurts, and my head too
variations.changed: which two parts

variations.cue: My hand has hurt for two days
variations.changed: yad is feminine, so tuʾlimunī — plus S02's duration

mistake.why: yad is feminine, so the verb is tuʾlimunī yadī. Body parts that come in pairs are usually feminine in Arabic, and the verb notices.

sentences.usage: How you list more than one complaint without sounding like a form — and the sentence that tests the agreement hardest.
sentences.mnemonic: One verb, two aches, one comma.

comprehensionPool.cue: My back has hurt for two days
I have a fever and a cough
I have a cold and I am not well
Do you have medicine for a headache?
I have to go to the doctor
The pharmacy is near the hospital
My stomach hurts, and my hand too
I have arrived at the hospital
